title: Breaking out of the god box | Greylock
gist: Greylock argues OpenAI's 'God Box' (ChatGPT, 1B+ users) is under-monetized as a consumer commerce front door because OpenAI is distracted by AGI/enterprise/data centers, leaving room for startups to break out via liability absorption, purpose-built product, or two-sided networks -- with AI primary-care doctors, AI wealth/tax advisors, and a social-game creator network cited as the first likely breakout categories in the next 18 months.

themes.theme: The God Box is beatable, not unbeatable

insights.claim: OpenAI's ChatGPT (the 'God Box') has over 1 billion users and reached that scale faster than any product in history, feeding a fear among investors that OpenAI has already won consumer AI outright.
insights.speaker: Seth Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Sets the bear case investors must underwrite against before backing any consumer-AI startup competing near OpenAI's core surface.
insights.quote: People are afraid that with over 1 billion users, OpenAI’s God Box has already won.

insights.claim: Greylock believes OpenAI's consumer commerce opportunity (positioning ChatGPT as the front door to all consumer commerce) is underestimated both by outside investors and likely by OpenAI's own team, because OpenAI's organizational attention is split across AGI research, enterprise sales, and data-center buildout.
insights.speaker: Seth Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Implies a window: capital and founders can target consumer AI commerce niches OpenAI is too distracted to prioritize, even though the prize is enormous.
insights.quote: OpenAI’s consumer opportunity is still underestimated by investors, and I suspect by their own team.

insights.claim: Because no single company captures an entire technology wave, some use cases will inevitably break out of OpenAI's ecosystem and become independent, venture-scale businesses even as ChatGPT dominates aggregate usage.
insights.speaker: Seth Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Core investment thesis: screen for startups attacking specific God-Box-adjacent use cases rather than betting against OpenAI head-on.
insights.quote: And one company rarely owns everything.

insights.claim: Greylock expects both the 'intelligent personal professional' category and 'networks for a new class of creators' to each produce generational (venture-outlier-scale) companies within the next 18 months, i.e., roughly by early 2028.
insights.speaker: Seth Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Gives investors a concrete timeframe to source and prioritize deals in these two categories before the window narrows.
insights.quote: We think both can produce generational companies in the next 18 months.

themes.theme: Framework: three ways to break out of the God Box

insights.claim: Startups can escape being absorbed into OpenAI's platform via 'liability absorption' -- taking on the licenses, capital, and legal risk (e.g., an AI bank or AI doctor) that a general model provider doesn't want to own, since delivering the end-to-end experience requires more than a strong model.
insights.speaker: Seth Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Regulatory/licensing-heavy verticals (banking, medicine, law) are structurally defensible moats against horizontal AI platforms.
insights.quote: Liability absorption. To provide the best end-to-end experience, you take on the licenses, capital and legal risk. An AI bank or doctor needs more than a strong model to get the job done.

insights.claim: A second escape path is a 'purpose-built product' -- a UI, workflow, or proprietary dataset that lives outside a general model's training set, making it hard for a horizontal assistant to replicate.
insights.speaker: Seth Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Investors should favor startups with proprietary workflow data/UI moats over thin wrapper products that a foundation-model chatbot could subsume.
insights.quote: Purpose-built product. A UI, workflow, or data that lives outside the training set.

insights.claim: A third escape path is enabling a two-sided network where matching and liquidity are the value driver (e.g., a career coach linked to an AI recruiter, or a dating coach linked to a matchmaker), since network effects are hard for a single-player assistant to internalize.
insights.speaker: Seth Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Marketplace/network businesses built on top of AI agents are a distinct, defensible category from single-user AI assistants.
insights.quote: Enables a two-sided network. Matching problems where liquidity wins. A career coach connected to an AI recruiter. A dating coach connected to a matchmaker.

insights.claim: AI is on track to replace the fleet of professional services once reserved for the wealthy (doctors, tutors, accountants, CFOs, wealth managers, executive assistants, lawyers, travel agents, therapists, career coaches, matchmakers, etc.) with AI equivalents available to everyone, and this trend is described as inevitable.
insights.speaker: Seth Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Broad TAM expansion thesis: any professional-services vertical is a candidate for an AI-native challenger; investors should map incumbents in each vertical for disruption risk.
insights.quote: This is inevitable.

insights.claim: OpenAI has an inherent advantage in the personal-professional category because consolidating all of a user's personal AIs in one place makes each individual assistant better (e.g., a personal trainer that also knows about a user's medical history via a shared context).
insights.speaker: Seth Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Explains why OpenAI's platform has a right to win in generalist assistant use cases -- competitors need a genuine data/liability moat to survive, not just a better UI.
insights.quote: It helps if your personal trainer knows about your neck injury.

insights.claim: Greylock's best guess is that the first intelligent personal professionals to break out at scale (independent of OpenAI) will be the AI primary care doctor and AI wealth/estate/tax advisor.
insights.speaker: Seth Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Directs deal sourcing toward AI health and AI wealth-management/tax startups as the highest-conviction near-term breakout categories.
insights.quote: Our best guess is the first intelligent personal professionals to break out at scale are the AI primary care doctor and AI wealth, estate, and tax.

insights.claim: OpenAI is already pursuing both AI healthcare and AI finance itself, evidenced by its acquisition of Hiro in finance and the launch of ChatGPT Health, but both markets remain open because the licensing and regulatory complexity involved doesn't fit OpenAI's platform model.
insights.speaker: Seth Rosenberg
insights.so_what: OpenAI's own moves into health/finance validate demand, but its reluctance to own full regulatory liability leaves room for licensed AI-native challengers in these two categories.
insights.quote: OpenAI recognizes this opportunity and are pursuing both, with their acquisition of Hiro in finance and launch of ChatGPT health. But both markets are still up for grabs.

insights.claim: AI primary care and AI wealth/estate/tax are attractive breakout categories in part because they sit atop the two largest wage/labor pools among the professional-services use cases discussed.
insights.speaker: Seth Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Sizes the addressable market by labor-cost displacement, a proxy investors can use to rank which AI-professional verticals are largest by revenue opportunity.
insights.quote: They also happen to sit on top of the two largest wage pools.

themes.theme: Creator networks and the AI 'camera filter' era

insights.claim: Historically, every major platform shift (mobile/internet, mobile camera, mobile GPS) has let amateurs create content or services that outcompeted incumbents, evidenced by Airbnb over hotels, Instagram/Snap over Kodak/Shutterfly, YouTube/TikTok/Reels over studios/Netflix, and Uber over taxis.
insights.speaker: Seth Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Pattern-matching framework: identify which AI-enabled amateur-creation category (games, music, software) will produce the next Airbnb/Uber/YouTube-style incumbent disruption.
insights.locator: Networks for a new class of creators

insights.claim: YouTube generated $40 billion in ad revenue in 2025, more than the combined ad revenue of the four major film studios, illustrating how amateur-creator platforms can eclipse legacy media incumbents in scale.
insights.speaker: Seth Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Concrete benchmark for how large a successful amateur-creator network can become relative to the legacy industry it disrupts -- a comp for sizing AI-native creator platforms.
insights.quote: That’s why YouTube’s $40bn in ad revenue in 2025 is larger than the ad revenue from the 4 major studios, combined.
insights.locator: Networks for a new class of creators

insights.claim: AI-enabled content creation today (turning natural language into music, video, and code via tools like Suno and AI code-gen) is at the equivalent stage of mobile evolution's early 'camera filter' era, not yet the breakout 'Instagram era' where a dominant two-sided network emerges.
insights.speaker: Seth Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Signals that the network-effect layer on top of generative-AI creation tools has not yet been built -- the real prize is still ahead, not in today's point-solution tools.
insights.quote: Today, AI evolution is at the equivalent of mobile evolution’s “camera filter” era, not yet its Instagram era.
insights.locator: So what new types of creation does AI enable?

insights.claim: Current AI creator tools (music, video, code generation) lack two-sided networks at scale, meaning the distribution/marketplace layer -- not the generation technology -- is the open opportunity for new entrants.
insights.speaker: Seth Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Investors should distinguish between generation-tool startups (commoditizing) and the eventual network/marketplace layer (the durable value capture point).
insights.quote: there are amazing creator tools that turn natural language into music, videos, and code. But no two-sided networks at scale.
insights.locator: So what new types of creation does AI enable?

themes.theme: Social gaming as the next breakout network

insights.claim: Greylock's best guess is that the first new two-sided AI creator network to break out at scale will be a social game platform, since AI code-gen now lets anyone turn natural language into playable games.
insights.speaker: Seth Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Flags social/UGC gaming as the highest-conviction near-term category for a new venture-scale creator network, ahead of AI music.
insights.quote: Our best guess is the first network to break out will be a social game platform.
insights.locator: Networks for a new class of creators

insights.claim: Musical.ly/TikTok took about 10 years to grow from a niche app to bigger than Hollywood using user-generated video, and Greylock expects user-generated games to overtake the games industry even faster given today's more mature AI creation tools.
insights.speaker: Seth Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Suggests a compressed timeline (faster than TikTok's decade) for a UGC-games platform to disrupt incumbents like EA and Activision -- a signal to watch for early traction metrics now.
insights.quote: Musical.ly/TikTok went from ridiculous to bigger than Hollywood in 10 years with user generated videos; user generated games can take over the industry much faster.
insights.locator: Our best guess is the first network to break out

insights.claim: A comparable breakout network in AI-generated music is considered less likely in the near term because listening habits are hard to shift away from Spotify until AI-generated music itself becomes bigger than traditional music or the consumption format changes.
insights.speaker: Seth Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Tempers enthusiasm for AI-music platforms (e.g., Suno-adjacent networks) relative to AI gaming as the nearer-term venture opportunity, since consumption-habit switching costs are the binding constraint, not generation quality.
insights.quote: it's harder to imagine consumption changing from Spotify until AI music becomes bigger than traditional, or the consumption format changes.
insights.locator: Music may spawn a network too

insights.claim: A successful AI game network would matter beyond entertainment: it is framed as a likely new source of livelihood for millions of entrepreneurs as traditional jobs are displaced by AI, and as a healthier form of social connection than today's algorithmic feeds.
insights.speaker: Seth Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Broadens the investment case for a UGC-game network beyond ad/engagement metrics to a labor-market and social-product thesis, which could support a larger long-term valuation ceiling.
insights.quote: An AI game network won’t just be big. It will be how the next millions of entrepreneurs earn a living as traditional jobs transition to new ones.
insights.locator: An AI game network won't just be big

insights.claim: The winning social-game network will need the same three structural components as Roblox -- an accessible game engine, a persistent identity/social graph spanning games, and a creator economy -- but must make the engine truly accessible to any amateur with an idea, not just semi-professional studios as on Roblox today.
insights.speaker: Seth Rosenberg
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete product checklist for evaluating AI-gaming startups: engine accessibility, cross-game identity/social graph, and creator monetization -- with amateur-accessibility as the key differentiator from Roblox.
insights.quote: The key difference is a game engine that’s truly accessible to anyone with an internet connection and an idea, not the semi-professional studios we see on Roblox.
insights.locator: The new social game network will have the same components
